opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core problem is that a lot of the things you care about only show up at scale, and the things you can cheaply measure at small scale don't always transfer. When you're running an experiment on a small model, you're getting a noisy, partial signal about what will happen when you train something a hundred or a thousand times bigger. Some changes look great at small scale and then the advantage washes out, or even reverses, as you scale up. Others look neutral or slightly worse early on and then turn out to matter a lot once the model has enough capacity to actually use them.

Part of that is just that the dynamics change. Optimization behaves differently, stability issues appear that you never saw in the small run, the model starts learning qualitatively different kinds of things. So you're trying to extrapolate along scaling curves, and you're betting that the slope you see at the small end continues, but you don't really know that until you've spent the compute.

And then there's the measurement side. At small scale the models are often too weak to show signal on the capabilities you actually care about, like reasoning or long-horizon tasks, so you end up using proxies such as loss or simpler benchmarks. Those proxies are correlated with what you want, but imperfectly.

So the real skill in research at a big lab is making good bets under that uncertainty. You've got a limited compute budget, you can't scale everything, and you have to decide which ideas get promoted to the next rung. A lot of research taste is basically having good intuitions about which small-scale results are real and which are artifacts, and designing experiments that de-risk the scale-up as cheaply as possible. It's a bit like being an investor: the information is always imperfect, and the question is how well you reason with it.

r001.rationale: It says some changes that look great on a small model can have their advantage wash out or even reverse as the model scales up.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the fundamental problem is that you can't actually run the experiment you care about. The thing you want to know is, does this change help at the scale where it actually matters, at the frontier run that's going to cost tens or hundreds of millions of dollars. And you obviously can't afford to run that experiment fifty times with fifty different variants. So what you do instead is run it at a scale that's orders of magnitude smaller, and then you have to make an inference.

And that inference is lossy in a bunch of ways. The most obvious one is that things just don't always transfer. There are architectural tweaks or optimizer changes that give you a nice bump at a small scale and then the gap closes or even reverses as you go up. Sometimes the small model is compute-bound in a way where the change is helping it use its limited capacity better, and once the model is large enough that's no longer the binding constraint. Other times it's the opposite, something looks neutral or slightly negative small and turns out to matter a lot at scale because it's fixing a problem that only shows up when you've got way more parameters or way more data flowing through.

Then there's noise. At small scale your runs are cheap, which is great, but the signal you're looking for is often really small. A half a percent improvement in loss might be what you're trying to detect, and seed variance alone can be comparable to that. So you have to be disciplined about running multiple seeds, about looking at scaling trends across several sizes rather than a single point, and about asking whether the slope is changing rather than just the intercept. Even then you're often left squinting at a plot and going, I think this is real.

And there's a more subtle thing, which is that the small-scale regime is just a different regime in terms of what the model is learning. The behaviors that we actually care about in the big models, the reasoning, the long context stuff, the way they generalize to things they weren't trained on, a lot of that barely exists at small scale. So your proxy metric, the loss on some held-out set, may be a fine proxy for some changes and a terrible proxy for others. If I'm testing a data mix change, the thing I care about might only show up in downstream evals that a small model can't even do.

So I think of it as evidence, genuinely useful evidence, but evidence with an unknown reliability that depends on what kind of change you're testing. The skill is partly in developing taste for which categories of intervention tend to transfer and which don't, and partly in structuring your experiments so you're measuring trends rather than points. And then you accept that occasionally you'll be wrong, and you build in the ability to notice that early in the big run rather than at the end.

r001.rationale: The response says some changes produce a bump at small scale but their gains close or reverse as scale increases.

astra-6.text:
Because the thing you actually care about is whether a change helps at the scale of your next big training run, and you’re testing it at a different scale. There’s no guarantee that the ranking of ideas stays the same. Something can look great on a small model and have its advantage disappear as you scale, or look fairly uninteresting initially and become useful at larger scale.

You’re also testing a whole configuration: the model, the amount of data, the learning rate, and how much effort you’ve put into tuning it. If a new architecture loses, is that because it’s worse, or because you haven’t found the right settings for it? You can spend more compute resolving that uncertainty, but then your cheap experiment becomes less cheap.

So small experiments are evidence. Ideally, you see a consistent improvement across several scales and have some reason to expect the trend to continue. But you’re still making a bet when you commit to the big run.

r001.rationale: The response says a small-scale advantage can disappear at larger scale, but does not clearly state that the change can worsen performance there.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the thing you actually care about is whether a change helps at the scale you’re going to train at, and a small experiment measures something slightly different. A change can look great on a small model because it helps that model use its limited capacity, and then the advantage disappears as you scale up. Or it can have overhead that makes it look bad at small scale, but that overhead becomes negligible for a large model.

So you’re trying to infer a trend from noisy measurements, and you don’t necessarily know whether the ranking of your experiments will stay the same. You can get more confidence by testing across multiple scales, but that costs compute too. There’s this tradeoff between spending more to find out which change is best and just spending that compute training the model you already know how to build.

r001.rationale: It says a small-scale advantage can disappear at larger scale, but does not state that the change can become worse than the baseline.
